name: Central Square Foundation (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: all CSF's work is in India.
summary: Central Square Foundation (CSF) supports Indian state governments' school reforms: the foundational literacy and numeracy missions of 11 states, new pre-primary classes, adaptive-learning software and other EdTech, school report cards for parents, and a pilot for high-potential students. We count its spending in the year to March 2026 against a year of those programmes' learning gains, credited by CSF's share of everyone's resources behind them (about 3% for the state missions, the largest branch) and valued as later earnings. At the defaults it comes to about 0.5 years of healthy life per $1,000, but the result is mostly uncertainty: how large the missions' learning gain is, how much of a test-score gain lasts into adult earnings, and the discount rate, since the earnings start a decade or more later. Every branch is discounted for missing data; adaptive learning has a randomised trial behind it, but no published effect size.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Students in the government schools of the 11 FLN states
rows.formula: fln_enrolled_as + fln_enrolled_br + fln_enrolled_gj + fln_enrolled_hr + fln_enrolled_mp + fln_enrolled_mh + fln_enrolled_od + fln_enrolled_pb + fln_enrolled_tn + fln_enrolled_ts + fln_enrolled_up
rows.explainer: The 11 states' counts summed (about 2.6 crore); the annual report's total across all 16 states and territories is about 2.85 crore.

rows.label: School grades the enrolment counts span
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most counts are UDISE+ enrolment in schools with Grades 1-5 (Punjab's and Tamil Nadu's are the FLN grades only); the FLN missions target Balvatika to Grade 3. Dividing by 4 (3 to 5) gives the children in one grade: each year one such cohort completes the foundational grades with the missions' gain.

rows.label: Children a year completing the foundational grades in the 11 states
rows.explainer: One cohort a year: a child's three or four years in the FLN grades produce one gain at the end of Grade 3, so a year of the missions is credited with one cohort's gain.

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per standard deviation of lasting learning (share of earnings)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, a placeholder until the site's shared figure for low- and middle-income countries lands (another build is adding it; this row is to be repointed to it). Anchor: across rich countries, one standard deviation more numeracy in adulthood goes with about 18% higher wages (Hanushek, Schwerdt, Wiederhold and Woessmann, 'Returns to skills around the world', European Economic Review 2015); in India's labour market, with more informal and agricultural work, likely lower. 15% (8% to 25%). The fade-out of a programme's gain is the next row.

rows.label: Share of an end-of-programme learning gain that lasts into adulthood
rows.explainer: Our judgment, a placeholder until the site's shared figure lands (to be repointed). Test-score gains fade: in Banerjee, Cole, Duflo and Linden's remedial-education trial in Indian cities (Quarterly Journal of Economics 2007) the gain shrank to about a third a year after the programme ended; long-run studies in the US find earnings effects larger than the faded test scores suggest (Chetty and others 2011). 40% (20% to 70%).

rows.label: Household sharing multiplier on an earnings gain
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure: an earnings gain is shared within the household.

rows.label: Years an earnings gain lasts, discounted
rows.explainer: A working life (the site's shared 40 years), discounted at the shared rate from when work starts.

rows.label: Units of value per unit of ln(earnings) gained for a working life, at the start of work
rows.explainer: Valued as later income on the site's scale ($uov_per_ln_consumption), like every model of childhood gains that pay off in adult earnings.

rows.label: Learning gain from the state FLN missions per child at the end of Grade 3 (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment of the missions' causal gain, net of trends and the post-pandemic recovery. Anchors: between 2022 and 2024 Std III reading in rural government schools, where the missions run, rose 7.1 percentage points (to 23.4%) against 2.4 in private schools, and arithmetic 7.4 against 4.4, 'substantially more than recovery' (ASER 2024 all-India presentation, slide 11, https://asercentre.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/ASER-2024-All-India-ppt-Jan-27-11am.pdf): the government schools' extra 3-5 points is about 0.1-0.17 SD on a normal scale; Uttar Pradesh, where CSF has worked since 2019, gained 15.6 points in reading and 20.6 in arithmetic since 2018 (annual report p. 30); structured pedagogy, the missions' model, is among the Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel's 'great buys' (2023 Smart Buys report). Government-run missions at state scale get less than trials do. 0.12 SD (0.04 to 0.25).

rows.label: Years from the end of Grade 3 to working age
rows.explainer: Children finish Grade 3 at about 8 and start earning at about 20 (later with more schooling, earlier in rural work): 12 years, from 10 to 14; the earnings gain starts after this wait, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Value of the FLN gain per child (units of value)
rows.explainer: The lasting share of the gain × earnings per SD, as ln(earnings), valued for a working life after the wait.

rows.label: FLN: value of a year's cohort gain in the 11 states, before adjustments
rows.explainer: One year's flow against one year's cost: the states' missions run every year, and CSF's support with them.

rows.label: Children who got pre-primary education for the first time in the reforms CSF supports

source.title: Central Square Foundation, Annual Report 2025-26, 'Learning to Build Tomorrow'
source.quote: ~4 lakh students received access to pre-primary education for the first time ever

rows.explainer: Balvatikas in Uttar Pradesh's government schools, Odisha's Sishu Vatika (about 3.2 lakh enrolled) and Telangana's 1,362 pilot schools (about 18,000), each with CSF's technical support (pp. 35-37). A year's enrolment against a year's support.

rows.label: Learning gain from a year of school-based pre-primary education (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. CSF's dipstick study of 134 Uttar Pradesh Balvatikas found children with a dedicated educator 13-17 points ahead on most tasks (pp. 35-36), but without random assignment; reviews of pre-primary programmes in low- and middle-income countries find school-readiness gains of roughly 0.1 to 0.3 SD, smaller where children would otherwise attend an anganwadi, as many here would. 0.15 SD (0.05 to 0.3).

rows.label: Years from pre-primary to working age
rows.explainer: Children in pre-primary are about 5-6 years old and start earning at about 20 (later with more schooling, earlier in rural work): 14 years, from 12 to 16, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Early childhood: value of a year's enrolment, before adjustments

rows.explainer: Children × the lasting gain valued as later earnings, as in the FLN branch.

rows.label: Learning gain from a year of personalised adaptive learning in government schools (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment from the trials. In Andhra Pradesh's randomised trial across 120 government schools (about 20,000 students in Grades 6-9, Kremer and the University of Chicago's Development Innovation Lab), PAL students gained 2.35 times as much as controls over 17 months, 'roughly 1.9 additional years of learning' (annual report p. 40; the working paper's effect in SD wasn't found). At the 0.1-0.2 SD a year of learning typical in Indian government middle schools, that is about 0.2-0.35 SD over 17 months; Mindspark, the same kind of software, raised scores by 0.37 SD in maths and 0.23 SD in Hindi in 4.5 months in Delhi (Muralidharan, Singh and Ganimian, American Economic Review 2019). Use falls at scale. 0.2 SD a year (0.1 to 0.35).

rows.label: Years from Grades 6-9 to working age
rows.explainer: Students in Grades 6-9 are about 11-15 years old (13 on average) and start earning at about 20 (later with more schooling, earlier in rural work): 7 years, from 5 to 9, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Adaptive learning: value of a year's use, before adjustments
rows.formula: pal_units_affected_per_year * ln(1 + pal_gain_sd * learning_persistence * earnings_gain_per_sd) * lnc_value_per_unit_gain * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -pal_years_to_work
rows.explainer: Students × the lasting gain valued as later earnings.

rows.label: Learners benefiting from the EdTech accelerator's product improvements

source.title: Central Square Foundation, Annual Report 2025-26, 'Learning to Build Tomorrow'
source.quote: reached over 55 lakh users, including more than 30 lakh learners who directly benefited from accelerator-driven innovations

rows.explainer: The LiftEd accelerator's 30 lakh learners (2023-2025, counted as a year's flow, a generous reading). EdTech Tulna's product reviews (56 lakh students in states' procurement) and AI Samarth's AI-literacy lessons (25 lakh learners) reach many of the same children with no measured learning effect; the small judged gain below covers them too.

rows.label: Learning gain per learner from better EdTech products and procurement (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the accelerator's quasi-experimental study (released April 2026) found positive effects of at-home EdTech on foundational learning (p. 40) but no figure is published; most of the gain is the products' own, and at-home use is light (Chimple in Ghaziabad: 62% of students active, 30-35 minutes a week, p. 41). CSF's part is the improvement over the products as they were. 0.01 SD (0.002 to 0.04).

rows.label: Other EdTech: value of a year's improvements, before adjustments
rows.formula: edo_units_affected_per_year * ln(1 + edo_gain_sd * learning_persistence * earnings_gain_per_sd) * lnc_value_per_unit_gain * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -fln_years_to_work
rows.explainer: Mostly primary-grade learners, so the FLN branch's wait to working age.

rows.label: Students in schools whose learning reports now go to parents (Jodhpur and Angul districts)

source.title: Central Square Foundation, Annual Report 2025-26, 'Learning to Build Tomorrow'
source.quote: ~1 lakh students covered by first-time competency-based assessments

rows.explainer: Jodhpur's 1,339 schools (about 70,000 students in Grades 6-9) and Angul's 1,362 schools (about 30,000 in Grades 5 and 8), where school-level report cards went to parents for the first time with CSF's support (pp. 44-45). Accreditation frameworks and state school standards authorities in six states have reached no parent yet: their effect would come through the same disclosure once it happens, and is not counted.

rows.label: Learning gain per student-year from school report cards for parents (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Report cards on every school in Pakistani villages raised test scores by about 0.11 SD, mostly through competition between private schools (Andrabi, Das and Khwaja, American Economic Review 2017); government schools with no rival nearby respond less, and a large school-quality programme in Madhya Pradesh had no effect on learning (Muralidharan and Singh 2020). 0.04 SD (0 to 0.11).

rows.label: Years from Grades 5-9 to working age
rows.explainer: Students in Grades 5-9 are about 10-15 years old (12 on average) and start earning at about 20 (later with more schooling, earlier in rural work): 8 years, from 6 to 10, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: School governance: value per student-year of disclosure (units of value)
rows.explainer: The lasting gain valued as later earnings.

rows.label: Share of the disclosure pilots that become lasting district practice
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Jodhpur expanded from 54 schools to the whole district and Odisha approved public disclosure of school reports, with a second pilot in about 700 schools (p. 45); but both rest on district collectors who move on, and NEP 2020's call for public disclosure has been slow to take hold. 50% (20% to 80%).

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer for how many years a won reform counts (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Years from the decision to the first report cards reaching parents
rows.explainer: Jodhpur's reports went to parents between September 2025 and March 2026 (p. 44); half a year, from 0 to 1.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

School governance: value of the disclosure reforms, before adjustments

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
Evidence adjustment: how far the learning-to-earnings chain should be trusted here
rows.explainer: Learning gains are measured on tests the states and partners often run themselves (administrative assessments can inflate), converted to standard deviations by our judgment, and carried to adult earnings by the shared-style figures above, which rest on rich-country wage data. Our judgment, 0.6 (0.35 to 0.9), below LEEP's 0.7 for the lead-to-IQ-to-earnings chain, which rests on cohort studies of the same outcome.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have come without CSF's support rather than another partner's
rows.explainer: The missions are national policy and would run without CSF; their gain is already credited to CSF only by its share of the resources. This row asks a different question: would another technical partner (Language and Learning Foundation, Pratham, consulting firms) have filled CSF's role, as several already work alongside it (Haryana: p. 20)? Our judgment, 85% (60% to 100%).

rows.explainer: Samagra Shiksha, through which the mission is funded, is shared 60:40 between the centre and most states and 90:10 for the north-eastern and Himalayan states (Assam among CSF's 11): 62% (60% to 70%) for CSF's states.

rows.label: CSF's 11 FLN states' share of India's government primary-school children
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the 11 states' counts sum to about 2.6 crore (rows above) against roughly 6.5 crore children in government primary grades nationally (UDISE+); they include Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, the two largest. 40% (30% to 50%).

rows.label: Other partners' yearly spending on FLN support in the same states (₹)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: other non-profits and funders work on the same missions (Language and Learning Foundation and Sampark in Haryana, Leadership For Equity, Pratham, Room to Read, Madhi Foundation; pp. 20, 23, 33), several on CSF's scale. ₹300 crore (₹150 to ₹600 crore) a year.

rows.label: CSF's own yearly spending on FLN, with its share of overhead (₹)
rows.explainer: FLN's share of all CSF's spending.

rows.label: FLN: CSF's share of the resources behind the missions' gain
rows.explainer: CSF's FLN spending over everyone's: the mission's central budget grossed up by the states' share and taken for CSF's 11 states, plus other partners'. Teachers' regular pay isn't counted: they were teaching anyway, and the gain is measured against schooling as usual.

rows.label: Early childhood: CSF's share of the resources behind the new pre-primary classes
rows.explainer: Our judgment: CSF's early-childhood spending (about ₹10 crore at its share above) against the states' — over 5,000 educators deployed in Uttar Pradesh alone (about ₹60 crore a year at contract pay), materials for 70,000 Balvatikas and 45,000 Sishu Vatikas, educators and helpers in Telangana's 1,362 schools — roughly ₹200-400 crore a year. 4% (2% to 12%).

rows.label: Adaptive learning: CSF's share of the resources behind the state deployments
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the states pay for devices, licences and teachers' time (about 4.3 lakh students), the University of Chicago's team ran the trial; CSF's technical support units in Andhra Pradesh and Himachal Pradesh are a few crore a year. 10% (4% to 25%).

rows.label: Other EdTech: CSF's share of the resources behind the product improvements
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the accelerator's grants and advice against the partner organisations' own spending on their products (Sesame Workshop India, ThinkZone, Top Parent, Chimple and others) and the states' procurement. 30% (10% to 60%).

rows.label: School governance: CSF's share of the resources behind the disclosure reforms
rows.explainer: Our judgment: CSF designed the assessments and report cards and ran them with the district administrations, whose staff and teachers carried them out. 50% (25% to 80%).

rows.label: High-potential students: CSF's share of the resources behind the pilot
rows.explainer: Our judgment: CSF funded and ran the accelerator with five partner organisations in Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti's schools. 50% (30% to 80%).

rows.label: FLN: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the children are the states' own counts, but the missions' gain is our judgment from national trends, not a controlled evaluation of CSF-supported implementation.

rows.label: Early childhood: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the gain is our judgment from other programmes and an uncontrolled comparison.

rows.label: Adaptive learning: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin, though close to measured: the students are the states' counts and a randomised trial of the same software in Andhra Pradesh's government schools exists, but its effect in standard deviations isn't published, so the gain per year is our conversion of its years of learning.

rows.label: Other EdTech: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no published effect for the improvements.

rows.label: School governance: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the effect is from a different setting (Pakistani villages' private schools).

rows.label: High-potential students: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no published effect size.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Each effect not modelled, with its sign: better learning keeps children in school longer and goes with later marriage and better health for their own children (+5%, 0 to +15%); civic and non-earnings value of literacy beyond wages (+2%, 0 to +5%); teachers' and mentors' time spent on data entry, assessments and app reporting instead of teaching, and pressure to report inflated results (-2%, -8% to 0). Net +5%, the parts' ranges combined: -5% to +20%.

rows.label: Total value (units of value)

rows.explainer: Each branch's value × its own adjustments, plus the side effects; money moved and career changes are zero.
